paragraphs: Friend, here's the big idea. Paul could have given an order, and he says so himself: in Christ he is "bold enough to order you to do what is proper" (Philemon 1:8). Instead he says, "I prefer to appeal on the basis of love" (Philemon 1:9). He wanted Philemon's goodness to come "by your own free will" (Philemon 1:14), because love that's forced isn't really love.

And look at what Paul asks for. Onesimus was a slave, and Paul asks Philemon to take him back "no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother" (Philemon 1:16). Paul even says, "charge it to my account" (Philemon 1:18), and he signs it with his own hand. I think that's a little picture of what Jesus did for us, taking on a debt that wasn't His so we could come home. When Jesus brings someone in, they become family, and everybody at the table gets a new way to see each other.

So what does this mean for you, baker? When you're in the right, you can still choose gentleness. When someone has hurt you and comes back changed, you can open the door wide, because God has already done that for you, and when you've got a hard conversation coming, go like Paul: warm words first, honest love, and room for the other person to say yes freely. I know what it's like to be called useless and then be made useful again, and that's what God does, and it never stops being wonderful.
